videos.title: What does a ‘Super El Niño’ mean for winter? | BBC News
videos.transcript: Could we get extreme weather, storms, floods, or even heavy snow this winter? As summer gives way to autumn, people start asking us the same questions. How bad could the weather get? When might we see the first snow? And just how cold would it be? This year, though, there's an extra factor in the mix, El Nino. [music] It could make this autumn and winter a little bit more interesting, at least from a weather perspective. So, what is El Nino? How could it affect the UK's weather? And is it something any of us should actually be paying attention to? Let's get into some of the biggest questions. Well, the first thing to say is that El Nino isn't a storm system. It's not going to bring sudden or noticeable impacts to any one place. Instead, it's a natural climate pattern that develops in the tropical Pacific Ocean. Sea temperatures rise, winds change direction, and that can influence weather around the world. It occurs every 2 to 7 years and that extra warmth generated in the Pacific is being released into the atmosphere where it can influence weather patterns all over the world bringing droughts, floods, heat [music] waves, and wildfires to different areas. Over the last few months, El Nino has been strengthening with sea temperatures rising into uncharted territory. Scientists predict that it will most likely be a historic event, the strongest ever recorded in the modern era. And because of this, you may have even heard people calling it a super El Nino or even [music] a Godzilla El Nino. Well, the name El Nino comes from Spanish and means little boy or the Christ child. South American fishermen and sailors in Peru and Ecuador first used the term centuries [music] ago when they noticed unusually warm waters appearing along the Pacific coast around December. Those warmer waters often meant fewer fish affecting their catches. And because the phenomenon tended to arrive around Christmas, it became known as El Nino. El Nino normally starts to develop in the late northern hemisphere spring and can continue to strengthen through the summer and autumn. This El Nino is expected to reach its peak in November or December and will last well into 2027. We start to see the impacts of El Nino in some parts of the world during the summer, such as the reduction in Atlantic hurricanes, the increase in Pacific hurricanes, and wildfires in Southeast Asia. [music] But further away from the tropical Pacific, impacts may not be felt until the northern hemisphere autumn or winter. It's looking likely that El Nino will affect the weather in the UK. The Met Office says that from around November onwards, there's an increased chance of stormier conditions affecting the UK. Wetter and windier weather could increase the risk of flooding and potential disruption or damage from strong winds. Chances are that it will also be milder than normal, at least for the first half of winter. It's too far away to know what will happen during the rest of winter, but during past El Nino events, the UK has often been colder than average, [music] and this could therefore increase the chances of frosts and snow. [music] But it's far from certain this will actually happen this year. So, does El Nino mean we're more likely to see snow on Christmas Day? Unfortunately, it's still too early to say. [music] What we do know is that of the three strongest El Nino events since 1900, only one in 198283 brought significant snowfall [music] to the UK. So, while El Nino can influence weather patterns around the world, it doesn't automatically mean a white Christmas is on the way. El Nino [music] impacts to the UK aren't as clear-cut as other parts of the world, so it's really difficult to assess how El Nino has affected the UK before. This is because the UK is located quite a long way from the tropical Pacific and there are many other weather patterns that influence our weather in the autumn and winter. However, we've looked at storminess in the UK during the last two strong El Ninos in 2023 24 and 2015 16 and we noted that we saw more named storms. So, wet and windy weather that was severe enough to bring significant impacts [music] in these two years than any other year since we started naming storms in 2015. And since 2000, looking at snowfall, less than half of the El Nino years brought [music] any significant snow to the UK. El Nino is likely to last into spring next year before it weakens during the summer. While there will be lots of obvious impacts in certain areas of the world, one of the largest global impacts is actually on the global average temperature. If you think of the warming seas in the Pacific Ocean like a radiator, when it heats up, the atmosphere warms up and it essentially boosts the global average temperature. Estimates are that they can add 0.2° C of extra heat over the year. Scientists therefore predict that 2027 will be the hottest year on record, exceeding the previous hottest year of 2024, which also happened to be the last time we had a very strong El Nino. More regionally with an increase in rainfall and floods in some areas and droughts in others. Agriculture will be impacted leading to a decline in global food supplies. The UN's World Food Program have already warned that El Nino will sharply increase hunger in more vulnerable parts of the world by the end of [music] 2027. Higher food insecurity will also mean higher prices in our supermarkets. With a likely increase in stormy weather and the potential increase in impacts from wind, rain, and flooding, we should keep a closer eye on the weather forecasts and be prepared to take action if the Metal Office issue any severe weather warnings. The UK government have also said that households should stock up on some food supplies to prepare for extreme weather. The idea being that if you are impacted by severe weather and you have some food supplies, it can keep you going for [music] a while longer before the emergency services can get to you and you're going to be a lot better off than if you haven't got supplies. So, there you have it. El Nino is continuing to strengthen and it's likely to be the biggest in living memory. While it won't hit as a sudden storm or event, it shifts the odds for more extreme weather around the world. Impacts in the UK will be felt later this autumn and through the winter with a greater chance of stormier weather at times. Globally, it will lead to higher average global temperatures, adding more heat on top of our already warming climate. And if there's any other weather subjects that you'd like us to tackle next, let us know in the comments.

videos.title: Why anxious French have cut back on spending
videos.transcript: French businesses are seeing customers play cautious on all sorts of things. Like when you go into a cafe, they say they're seeing customers uh share desserts and uh and starters and that sort of thing. They're cutting back on wine. Um, and what they say is that they feel that people are really being squeezed by higher energy prices, higher inflation, and there's also on top of that, there's just a general anxiety about the state of the economy and where it's going with a presidential election next year that at this point is still very much uncertain. Weak consumer spending in France is is an issue because the French economy is very much a consumerdriven uh economy. Consumer spending makes up about half of of GDP. And not only that, but it's also the biggest single source of of revenue for the government through the value added tax. Um so uh when consumer spending slows, that's less tax revenue for the government. And the government is desperately in need of all source of income that it can get its hands on at this point because it's has one of the highest budget deficits in the European Union. and it faces a very tumultuous passage of the 20 27 budget in the parliament in the coming weeks because the parliament is very divided amongst the very different parties. This could impact next year's presidential election. It can affect it in two ways. There's firstly um the the fact that nobody really knows where the country is going to be going uh after the election. That's a source of of uncertainty. People don't know how that will affect taxes, for example, and taxes are already very high in France. So any if there's an increase in tax or a decrease in tax, that will have a very big impact on people. And then secondly, that means that the the candidates, they all have to address the issue of declining purchasing power in their programs one way or another. Some are proposing tax cuts on payroll tax in particular, which are very high and which are one of the reasons why purchasing power is so reduced in France. And others are calling on on companies to just simply increase wages. But uh the fact is whatever is done, the government has very little leeway to uh reduce taxes or spend more to to improve people's purchasing power.

videos.title: Is Europe ready for more heatwaves?
videos.transcript: Record-breaking temperatures, wildfires, and droughts. Is Europe ready for this? Is it prepared, or is this simply the new normal? Andrea, I'm going to start with you. >> Let me say that we have had 150 million people affected by the heatwave over the last couple of weeks, and we lost 1,300 people. And I think this loss shows us we are not yet prepared. We are doing everything now which is in our hands to collide to find these issues at a European level, but no, we are not where we need to be to protect people in Europe. >> Why are we not prepared? This is not the first time we had a heatwave. >> extreme weather in the summer, we have extreme weather in the autumn. I want I want to remember Valencia, I want to remember the flooding also in Italy. We have extreme weather also in the winter. This is a pattern, it's a climate pattern, and we're not prepared because there's a lot of people in this parliament and in many institutions that still think that climate change is not an issue. And if we do not respond to this extreme condition in a systemic way, we will never be prepared.
